*krumba- ~ *krumpa- 307

*krumba- ~ *krumpa- adj. ‘crooked, bent’ — OE crump adj. ‘id.’, OS krumb
adj. ‘id.’, Du. krom adj. ‘id.’, OHG krumpf, krumb adj. ‘id.’, MHG krumpf, krump
adj. ‘id.’, G krumm adj. ‘id.’ (DRV).

An adjective derived from the strong verb *krimpan- (q.v.). In view of the
variant *krumba-, this verb must have replaced the more primary *krimban-
< *gré-m-b'-e- under the influence of the iterative, cf. G krumpfen w.v. ‘to
cringe’ < *krumb/pon- < *grmb'-néh2-.

*krunkon- w.v. ‘to wind’ — EDu. kronken w.v. ‘id.’, Du. kronkelen w.v. ‘to
wind, squirm’ > *grng*-néhz- (DRV?).
The iterative to *kringan- ~ *krinkan- (q.v.).

*kruppa- m. ‘compact object’ — ON kroppr m. ‘body, trunk’, Far. kroppur m.
‘body, build; corpse’, Sw. krupp m. ‘body’, OE crop m. ‘sprout, bunch, rock’, E
crop, MDu. crop(pe) m. ‘gnarl, bud, rosette; body; goiter’, Du. krop m. ‘goiter;
rosette (of lettuce)’, OHG kropf m. ‘goiter’, G Kropf m. ‘id.’ (DRV?).

An a-stem perhaps related to *krupp/bon- (q.v.) through a meaning ‘to be
clump-like’.

*krupp/bon- w.v. ‘to crawl’ — MDu. cropen w.v. ‘id.’, G Rhnl. kruppen ‘to
crouch, curl up’, Cimb. kruppen ‘to crawl’ > *grub*-néh2- (NEUR) — Lith.
grubinéti ‘to stumble’ < *grub*-nh2- plus the stative suffix *-ehz-.

The iterative to *kreupan- ~ *krupan- (q.v.), closely related to OE cryppan
wv. ‘to bend’, G kriipfen, krupfen w.v. ‘to bend’, refl. ‘to cringe’ < *kruppjan-.
Cimb. kruppen goes back to a variant *krubbon-, not *krubjan- with checking
of the umlaut (cf. Cimb. hiiffen ‘hiipfen, saltettare’ < *huppjan-), and the dou-
ble *b reveals that the original IE consonantism was *b* instead of *b. It
arose analogically when the original iterative paradigm 3sg. *kruppopi, 3pl.
*krubunanpi < *grubh-néh2-ti, *grub*-nh2-énti was split up into 1) *kruppopi,
*krupunanpi (cf. MDu. cropen) and 2) *krubbopi, *krubunanpi (= G obs.
kroben, DWB: 11, 2347). Note that the iterative has a parallel in Lith.
grubinéti, and therefore can be old. See also *krup(p)ila-.

*krup(p)ila- adj. ‘cripple’ — ON kryppill adj. ‘id.’, Far. krypil adj. ‘id’, OE
crypel adj. ‘id.’, MDu. cropel adj. ‘id.’, Du. kreupel adj. ‘id.’ (DRV).

An adjective derived from the verb *kreupan- ~ *kriipan- (q.v.) with the
usual *-ila- suffix. The double p of ON kryppill has always been difficult to
account for, because it points to *kruppila- rather than the more wide-
spread *krupila-. The issue can be resolved, however, by assuming that
*kruppila- was derived from the strong verb *kreuppan- before the short-
ening of the geminate. The geminate may then have been analogically re-
moved on the basis of the singulated form *kreupan- in all languages except
Icelandic. See also *krupp/bon-.

308 *kruppjan-

*kruppjan- w.v. ‘to bend, stoop’ — OE cryppan wv. ‘to bend’, G kripfen,
krupfen w.v. ‘to bend, refl. to cringe’ (DRV).
A causative derived the iterative *krupp/bon- ‘to crawl’ (q.v.).

*krutt/d6n- ww. ‘to pack(?)’ — Nw. kroda w.v. ‘to huddle (around)’, krota
w.v. ‘to coagulate, curdle’, ME crudden wv. ‘to coagulate, congeal, solidify,
curdle’, G obs. krotten wv. ‘to swell’, Swi. xrotten w.v. ‘to pack, stuff (DRV?).

An iterative 3sg. *krutton, 3pl. *krudunanpi related to *kreudan- ~
*kridan- (q.v.). In view of the meaning of G krotten ‘to swell’, it is possible
that the etymologically obscure *krud(d)6n- ‘toad’ (q.v.) was derived from
it. The German verb is further reminiscent of W chrothi ‘to bulge’ and the
pertaining W crwth, croth f. ‘bulge, belly, womb, calf of the leg, violin’, Olr.
cruit ‘hump; harp’ < *krutt-, which has previously been derived from VLat.
crotta ‘crypt, vault’ < crypta (Meid 1970: 138, fn. 74, 76). Can the Celtic
forms be explained by borrowing from Germanic?

*kuban- m. ‘shed’ — ON kofi m. ‘convent cell; hut, shed’, Far. kovi m. ‘out-
building’, Elfd. kuvi m. ‘chamber’, OE cofa m. ‘chamber, cave, den’, MDu. cove
m. ‘hut, shed’, MHG kobe m. ‘stable’ (also kobel m. ‘shed, box’), G Koben m.
‘shed’ => *gub-on-(?) (GM).

Formally close to, but irreconcilable with Gr. yom ‘hut’, which has a long
upsilon from -uH- (if the word is of IE origin). The alternative comparison
with Av. gufra adj. ‘deep, hidden’ < *gup-ro- and OCS Zupa f. ‘grave’ <
*geup-ehz- is not attractive either, because the Germanic word must have
originally meant “wattle shed”, cf. MDu. cubbe f. ‘weir, basket, reed roof’, Du.
kub (cf. EDu. kubbingh ‘shed of reed’) < *kubj6-. Also cf. OHG kubisi n. ‘cot-
tage’ < *kubesja-.

*kuddan- m. ‘bag’ — ON koddi m. ‘pillow’, Far. koddi m. ‘id.’, Nw. kodd(e) m.
‘pillow; scrotum, testicle’, OSw. kodde m. ‘testicle’, OE codd m. ‘bag, scrotum;
husk’, EDu. kodde ‘testicle’ (GM).

The n-stem *kuddan- looks like a hypocorism to the full-grade formation
OE céod m.f. ‘pouch’, OHG kiot m. ‘id.’ < *keuda-. Perhaps Swab. Kotz f. ‘pim-
ple, blister(?)’ can be adduced to reconstruct an n-stem variant *kutt6n-.

More certain is the connection with ON kodri m. ‘scrotum’ < *kudran- and
MDu. codde, EDu. kodde ‘cudgel’, Scot. cud ‘staff, club’ < *kuddan-.

*kudja- n. ‘herd’ — OFri. kedde m. ‘id’, MDu. cudde n./f. ‘id’, Du. kuddec
‘id.’, OHG kutti n. ‘id’, G Bav. kutt n./f. ‘flock of birds’ > *gh3-u-d"h;-io- (IE).
No existing etymology: the connection with *kuddan- ‘bag’ (Pokorny IEW:
393-8) cannot be maintained. As the word may originally have applied to
cow herds, I propose to reconstruct the word as PIE *g¥h3-u-d*h;-io-, lit.
meaning “set of cows”. With this reconstruction, the word would be fully

*kukjan- 309

parallel to *awidja- ‘flock of sheep’ < *h3eui-dth;-io-. Note that the IE word
for ‘cow’ (see *k6- ~ *ku-), is likely to have been derived from a root *g¥eh3-
‘to keep’, cf. Gr. Béoxw ‘to feed, tend, pasture’ < *gh3-ske-, and that this
verb was not necessarily restricted to the grazing of cows.

*kukjan- wv. ‘to kiss’ — Go. kukjan w.v. ‘id.’, LG ktikken wv. ‘id.’, Du. dial.
kukken w.v. ‘id.’ (GM).
An originally onomatopoetic formation parallel to the verb *kussjan-

(qv.).

*kula- 1 n. ‘cool wind’ — ON kul, kol n. ‘id.’ > *glH-o- (DRV).

A zero-grade formation to the strong verb *kalan- (q.v.). The vocalization
of the resonant may point to a root-final laryngeal. Also cf. Far. kyling f.
‘breeze’.

*kula- 2 n. ‘coal, charcoal’ — ON kol n.pl. ‘id.’, Far. kol n. ‘id.’, Elfd. kuol n.
‘id’, OE col n. ‘id.’, E coal, OFri. kole f. ‘id.’, MDu. cole m./f. ‘id.’, Du. kool n./c.
‘id.’, OHG kol n., kolo m. ‘id.’, MHG kol n. ‘id.’, G Kohle f. ‘id’ => *gulH-o- (1E?) —

A strong verb with two ablauting variants, viz. *kweman- and *kuman-.
This alternation may point to the pre-existence of an athematic present 3sg.
*gvém-ti, 3pl. *g¥m-énti. Since, however, the presentic formations in the

grades in Go. giman and OHG queman (cf. Seebold 1970: 315). See also
*kwumpi-.

An adjective with two different proto-forms: EGm. *kwiwa- and NWGm.

The best way of dealing with *kwikwa- is to start from an originally redu-

cess, or restored the reduplication at a later stage. The reduplication itself
seems to have originated in the verb *g™i-gvh3-é-, cf. Skt. jivati, YAv. juuaiti,
Gr. (aw, Lat. vivé, OCS Ziti (Zivg) ‘to live’ < *gihzu-e- < *gi-gh3-e- (again
with dissimilation of the second velar).

(q.v.). In WGm., we further find a denominative *kwikw6jan-: OE cwician, OS
quikon ‘to cause to live’, Du. kweken ‘to grow (crops)’.

*luka- 343

A European word for ‘lynx’. The form */uhsa- corresponds to the feminine

*madron- f. ‘madder’ — ON madra f. ‘id.’, Nw. modre f. ‘id.’, OE mzdere,

354 *manniska-

*dhghm-on- (IE) — Lat. hom6, -inis m. ‘human being, man’, Lith. obs. Zmud m.
‘man’, OPru. smoy ‘id.’ < *d*ghm-on-; Lith. Zmogus m. ‘man’ (for the suffix, cf.
OCS mo-Zb ‘man’ < *mon-gb-io-).

A word that was inflected as an n-stem in the singular and as a root noun
in the plural. Presumably, the original paradigm *manno, pl. *mannaniz
developed into *mann6, *manniz by regular Proto-Germanic syncope of the
unstressed vowel in the sequence *-nnan-. The n-stem endings were then
removed from the singular in most languages except for Gothic and OE
manna. The etymology of the word is disputed. Some connect Skt. mdnu-
‘man’ (cf. Ringe 2006: 139), but the underlying formation *men-u- (not
*mon-u-) would regularly give *minn- in Germanic. It is therefore more
likely that the word split off from the PIE word for man, viz. *d*g*m-on-,
which is the form underlying the parallel formation *guman- ‘man’ (q.v.).
The accusative stem *d*ghm-on- regularly lost the initial stops, the initial
cluster Cm- being impossible in Germanic, and thus gave rise to a PGm. root
*man- (Berneker 1898: 360-1). The geminate probably arose secondarily in
an analogical paradigm nom. *man6o, gen. *mannaz < quasi-PIE *mén-on,
*mon-n-6s. See further also *manniska-.

*meltja- n. ‘milt, spleen’ — ON milti n. ‘id.’, Far. milt(i) n. ‘id.’, Nw. milte n.

-jo- is the regular outcome of u-breaking of e. The confusion between o and

A strong verb related to *meluka-, *mulkna-, *mulki- and *mulk6n- (q.v.).

366 *méri-

*méri- adj. ‘famous’ — Go. waila-mers adj. ‘with a good reputation’, ON

A vrddhi-gerundive to a further unattested strong verb *meran-, cf. Icel.

*muwi- f. ‘mosquito’ — OSw. mygga f. ‘id.’, OE mycge f. ‘id.’, E midge, WFri.

Also cf. ON my n. ‘mosquito’ < *muja- and Sw. mygg n. ‘id.’ < *mujja-. The

can thus be reconstructed as *muwi, *mujjéz, continuing PIE *muH-fha,
*muH-iéhz-s. Note that the short *u in Gm. arose due to the operation of
Dybo’s law of pretonic shortening. For a parallel development, see *bruwi-
‘bridge’.

*nepan- s.v. ‘to grant safety(?)’ — Go. niban sv. ‘to unite (in consanguinity),
help’ = *nét-e- (IE) — Perhaps to ToA nati, ToB nete ‘might, strength’ <

The evidence clearly implies a PIE root *net-, which finds an excellent
parallel in PTo. *nete (Adams 1999: 342). Within Germanic, I consider
*nepja- ‘relative’ < *net-io- to be cognate. The original meaning of the word
must have been ‘to offer protection’, i.e. to relatives and people within the
clan. See further *népo-.

*nepja- m. ‘relative’ — Go. nibjis m. ‘kinsman’, ON nidr m. ‘son, kinsman,
relative’, OE nibpas, nipas m.pl. ‘men’ > *nét-io- (IE).

The word is often derived from PIE *nep-t-io- (for which see *nefan-
‘nephew, cousin’), but the implied cluster reduction is ad hoc and must be
rejected. Equally uncertain is the connection with Skt. nitya- adj, ‘innate’. In
my view, the likeliest scenario is that the word was derived from the PIE
root *net- as found in PGm. *nepan- ‘to offer protection’ (q.v.). Presumably, a
PIE *net-io- was a clan-member, i.e. someone under the patron’s protective
sphere. A possible feminine form *nepjo- can be identified in the MDu. suffix
-nede, swasenede ‘sister-in-law’ < *swésa-nepj6- and enede ‘wife’ <
*aiwo-nepjo- (but see *magapi- for a different explanation).

*ohs(t)no- f. ‘armpit’ — OE oxn f. ‘id’, OHG uohsana f. ‘id.’ (IE).

least superficially seems to reflect *hzh1-es-ds (cf. Rieken 1999: 186) with

the reversed order of the laryngeals. Kloekhorst 2008: 166, on the other

*pakka- n. ‘bundle, pack’ — ME packe ‘id.’, E pack, MLG pack n. ‘id.’, MDu.

A “Middle Germanic” word with an obscure prehistory. The restriction of

theoretically have served as the source of the Germanic word. The alterna-

*saipwon- f. ‘soap’ — OE sdpe f. ‘id.’, E soap, OFri. sépef. ‘id.’, Du. zeep c. ‘id.’,
OHG seiffa, seipfa f. ‘id.’, G Seife, Swab., Alem. seipfe f. ‘id.’ (GM).

An etymologically debated word with an exclusively West Germanic at-
testation (ON sdpa is an Old English loanword). Two formations have been
reconstructed for Proto-Germanic: 1) a form *saipjén- with aj-suffix so as to
explain the gemination OHG seipfa, Swi. seipfe; and 2) a form *saip6n- in
order to explain the absence of umlaut in OE sdpe. Superficially, the form
*saipjon- is corroborated by Fi. saippio, but I would prefer to unify both OHG
seipfa and OE sape into a single proto-form *saipwon-. This form can explain
both the lack of umlaut in Old English and the gemination in High German,
and even has a reminiscence in Fi. saippua (note that the io-suffix of saippio
can be of Finnish origin, Koivulehto 1995: 99). The derivation of the word is
unknown, but the parallel occurrence of the semantically more primitive OE
sdp(e) ‘amber, resin’ (also cf. OE stdr-sép n. ‘resin’ < *saipja-) implies a
Germanic origin. The suggested link with e.g. Sw. dial. sipa w.v. ‘to flow
slowly’ (cf. Pokorny IEW: 894) is uncertain, however. Lat. sdpo m. ‘soap’
was borrowed from Germanic.

426 *sambu-

Most forms point to *sanda-, but MHG sampt can only be explained from

view of the meaning ‘sand’, it is extremely unlikely, at any rate, that the
word spread across Europe as a Wanderwort. Importantly, this scenario
implies that other NIE words with the same nd‘)-suffix (e.g. *arwit ‘pea’)
probably cannot be regarded as relatively late Wanderworter either, but are
likely to have been present in Europe already before the arrival of the In-
do-Europeans.

An adjective continuing the participle of the IE verb ‘to be’, viz. *hs-ont-.
If we accept Lat. iéns, gen. euntis ‘going’ < *hyi-(e)nt-s, *hii-ont-es as a model,
we may reconstruct the original paradigm of this participle as *his-(e)nt-s,
gen. *his-ont-(e/o)s. Germanic generalized the o-grade at an early stage,
however (cf. Go. -ands). The original meaning ‘being’ developed into ‘true’ in
Germanic, probably through an intermediate sense ‘actual’. The meaning

Lat. sons must have developed at an early stage, possibly in a shared IE legal

sanna, senna w.v. ‘to dispute’ < *sanpdjan-. See also *sunja-.

An old o-grade thematicization to the PIE root *seu-. The form is of im-

Sagum n. ‘coarse woollen cloak’ may be a Gaulish loanword,
Walde/Hoffmann: II, 464). A third possibility would be to assume a connec-
tion with Icel. seg/ n. ‘piece of wood in the eye of a grinding mill’ < *segla-,
Far. sigli n. ‘id.’ < *seglja- (= G dial. Segel, Sigel m. ‘lump’?). This would imply
a primary meaning ‘mast’.

The PIE numeral ‘six’. The oldest form must have been *uek-s in view of

Most Germanic languages, including Gothic, have a form continuing a
proto-form *sehstan-. This form replaced the more archaic *sehtan-, as
evinced by ON sétti and OHG sehto, under the influence of the cardinal nu-
meral *sehs. In PIE, the oldest form was *uk-to- (without both initial and
root-final s), cf. OPru. uschts. It follows that *s(uJek-tHo- arose due to inter-
ference with *sept-m ‘seven’ (see PGm. *sebun).

*skeutan- s.v. ‘to shoot, dash’ — ON skjota sv. ‘id.’, Far. skjdta sw. ‘id.’, Elfd.

A strong verb usually connected to Skt. skundate ‘to jump’, which, how-

wv. ‘to swing, shake’ < *skaddén- and Nw. skata w.v. ‘to push, drive’ <
*skaton-. As a result, all older etymological connections based on the

cédati ‘to push’ < *k™eud- or Alb. hedh, hjedh ‘to throw’ < *ske(ujd-, can be
dropped. See also ON skjétr, OE scéot adj. ‘fast’ < *skeuta-, *skauta- and

Du. schooien w.v. ‘to hang around, go around begging’ < *skaujan-. Also cf.
*skehan- (< *skékw-e-?).

448 *skrimman- ~ *skrimpan-

Du. schrikken s.v. ‘to be startled’, OHG screck6n w.v. ‘to jump’, MHG schricken
wv. ‘id.’ (GM).

The oldest attestations all point to a weak verb *skrikk6n-, which in MHG
and MDu. seems to have become strong in intransitive use, cf. MHG
schrecken, pret.3sg. schrak, 3pl. schraken, ptc. ge-schrocken and Du.
schrikken, pret. schrok, ptc. ge-schrokken. It in turn gave rise to the transi-
tive verb MHG schrecken w.v. ‘to startle’, Swi. (Visp.) Srekxu ‘to tear’ (< ‘to
make burst’, cf. G sprengen), apparently from PGm. *skrakkjan-. The original
meaning of the verb was ‘to jump’, cf. OHG hewi-skrecko, G Heu-schrecke m.
‘grasshopper’ < *hauja-skrikkan-, lit. “hay-hopper”. No certain etymology.
The connection with Olr. scréoin ‘startling’, which has been derived from
*skreg-ni-, must be abandoned because this meaning is secondary in Ger-
manic.

*skrimman- ~ *skrimpan- s.v. ‘to contract’ — OE scrimman s.v. ‘to shrink,
contract’, MDu. schrimpen s.v. ‘id.’, MHG schrimpfen s.v. ‘to shrivel’ >
*skrémb'-e- (NEUR) — Close to Lith. skrébti (skrembwu) ‘to shrink’ <
*skre-m-bh-e-.

A strong verb based on a nasalized root *skre-m-b*-, which gave *skrimm-
through a form *skrémb'-ne-. The variant *skrimpan- arose due to influence
from the iterative *skrumpon- (q.v.). See also *skrinkwan-.

*skrinkwan- s.v. ‘to shrivel’ — Nw. skrokka s.v. ‘to shrivel’, OE scrincan s.v.
‘to shrink up, dry up, dwindle’, E to shrink, EDu. schrincken ‘to cringe, re-
treat’ (GM).

A strong verb (cf. OSw. skrunkin, Elfd. skrukken, Nw. skrokken pte. ‘shriv-
eled’), not to be confused with the weak Far. skrykkja w.v. ‘to wrinkle; to
pull, tug’, Elfd. skryttja w.v. ‘to shrivel; to cringe’ < *skrunkjan- (derived
from *skrunkwa-, cf. Nw. skrukk m. ‘wrinkle’). G schrincken is assumed to be
an adaptation of E to shrink (DWB: 15, 1754) by the poet Georg Rudolf
Weckherlin (1584-1653), who worked in England for a couple of years, but
EDu. schrincken appears to be native. No clear etymology. Perhaps there is a
link with ME shruggen ‘to shiver, shudder; to move about’, E to shrug, which
is also attested with the meaning ‘to cringe’, and Sw. dial. skrukka, skruga
w.v. ‘to stoop’ < *skrukk/gon-, which is suggestive of a root *skrek- or
*skregh-. See also *skrankwjan-.

*skripan- ~ *skridan- s.v. ‘to stride’ — ON skrida ‘to creep, crawl’, Far.
skrida s.v. ‘id’, Elfd. skraida s.v. ‘to pace’, OE scridan s.v. ‘to go, take one’s

*skura/6- 451

No clear etymology. The verb has been equated with *skupp/bén- 2 ‘to
shove’ (q.v.) through an intermediate meaning ‘to jump, frolic’, but this se-
mantic shift is not supported by the attested forms. I rather assume that
*skupp/bon- was formed to the root *skep- ‘to mock’. However, since the
implied proto-form *skp-nehz- would not regularly yield PGm. *skupp/bon-,
it must be assumed that the *u represents a secondary zero-grade. Also cf.
ON skaup n. ‘mocking’ < *skaupa-, ON skop n. ‘id.’, OS skop-liko adv. ‘poeti-
cally’, MDu. schop n. ‘jest’, OFri. schof n. ‘mocking’ < *skup(p)a- / *skuffa- and
OE scop, OHG scof, scopf m. ‘poet’ < *skuppa-. Note that OFri. skof together
with E to scoff < *skuff- proves that the original root-final consonant must
have been an *fcontinuing Pre-Gm. *p.

*skura/o- m./f. ‘short shower (of rain/hail)’ — Go. skura f. ‘id.’, ON skur f.
‘id’, Far. skdrur m. ‘id.’, Elfd. skaur f. ‘id.’, OE scur m. ‘id.’, E shower, MDu.
schuur m./f. ‘id.’, OHG skur m. ‘id.’, G Schauer m. ‘id.’ (GM).

Also cf. Nw. skgyre, skjgre f. ‘gust of wind’ < *skaurjén- and skyra w.v. ‘to
take off quickly’ < *skurjan-. De Vaan 1999 compared the word to PGm.
*skur- ‘to cut, tear’, but in view of OS skion m. ‘cloud’, 1 propose to recon-

*skéhy-ur, gen. *skhz-un-ds (in view of the absence of Dybo’s law, the accent
must have shifted to the stem at an early stage). It was derived from the

Skt. chaya- f. ‘shadow, reflection’, Gr. oxud f. ‘shade’, Alb. hie f. ‘shade, shad-

thus imply a third stem variant *sku(w)en- that may originate from the da-
tive form *sku(w)eni. Unrelated to Lat. caurus m. ‘north wind; north-west
wind’ < *Khuer-o-, Lith. Siduré ‘North’ < *Kehyur-io- and OCS sévere ‘North;
north wind’, Ru. séver ‘North’, SCr. sjévér m. ‘id.’ < *Kehiuer-o-.

452 *skuwwan-

*skot-ske-; Lat. scatd, -ere ‘to gush forth, swarm’ < ‘*skt- (with
schwa-secundum, De Vaan 2008: 543-4).

The iterative to *skeutan- (q.v.). In view of the o-grade variants MHG
schatten wv. ‘to swing, shake’ and Nw. skata ww. ‘to push, drive’ <
*skat(t)6n- < *skot-nehz-, the *u of *skut(t)On- must be analyzed as a sec-

back-formation to the iterative, something that is also implied by Swi. Sutz

be corrected to *sket-. This root is reconcilable with Lith. skdsti ‘to jump’ <

*smérjon- f. ‘clover’ — Icel. smeraf. ‘id’, Far. smera f. ‘id.’, Nw. smzre m./f.

The IE word for ‘sun’, ie. an old heteroclitic noun originally inflected as

stealthily’, which is especially prominent in reflexive uses of the verb, cf.

*stén- s.v. ‘to stand’ — Far. poet. std suppl.v. ‘id.’, Nw. std suppl.v. ‘id.’, OSw.

A verb in suppletion with *standan- (q.v.). The verb is not attested in the
oldest Germanic languages, but its occurrence in both North and West Ger-

old age of the NGm. verb, cf. Nw. dial. (Selbu) std with Proto-Norse nasaliza-

difficulties, however. Many of the forms can be derived from PGm. *stén-, i.e.
a verbum purum or root present. This reconstruction can only be reconciled
with the PIE root *stehz-, however, by positing a Narten-present 3sg.

the rise of PNWGm. *std-, unless one is willing to accept a PGm. change
*-aja- > *-d- (Pérhallsddéttir 1993: 35-6). Inspecting the modern dialects
does not help much. Swi. Appenzell 3sg. stéd, 3pl. stént, Sténd probably
points to *stépi, *sténdi, but the lack of umlaut in the singular and its pres-
ence in the plural is the opposite of what is expected. In Dutch, Stellingwerf
staon (with ao < PGm. *é) points to *sté-, but Sliedrecht staon (with ao from
lengthened *a) to *sta-. Anyhow, Seebold 1970: 464-5 probably correctly
starts from *stén- adopting the view that it arose due to analogy to *gén- ‘to

go’.

*takan- ~ *tékan- s.v. ‘to touch’ — Go. tekans.v. ‘id.’, ON taka s.v. ‘to take; to
reach, touch’, Far. taka s.v. ‘id.’, Elfd. tégd s.v. ‘to take; to hit’, MDu. taken
wv. ‘to take, seize’ => *thzg-e- (IE/DRV?) — ToB tdak- ‘to touch’ < *thzg- (with
secondary d after the full grade cek- < *tég- < *te-th2g-?); Gr. tetaywv ‘tak-
ing’ < *te-thzg-ont-.

The Germanic strong verb is clearly derived from PIE *tehzg-, but the
development of this root into *takan- and *tékan- is not straightforward. An
important problem is the ablaut difference between Go. tekan and ON taka.
The later form seems to continue a tuddti-formation with zero grade of the
root, viz. *thzg-é-, but Go. tekan cannot regularly be derived from the
full-grade *téhzg-e-, as this would give **tdkan-. The greatest difficulty,
however, consists of the irregular correspondence of PGm. *t- with PIE *t-.
It has been suggested that the t arose in reduplicated root *te-thzg-, cf. Gr.
tetaywv. As laryngeals do not vocalize in unstressed syllables, this stem
would yield a PGm. form *tedg- in which the reduplication may have been
restored (Mottausch 1993). The long *é can subsequently be explained as
from a form *dehig- that developed out of *dedg- by dissimilation of the
second (glottalized) *d (Kortlandt 2000). An alternative explanation would
be to assume that *tékan- was back-formed to the iterative *pak(k)6n- <
*thzg-néhz-, as a-grade iteratives give rise to secondary reduplicated verbs
more often, cf. *slépan- ‘to sleep’ from *slapp/bon- (q.v.).

*tibra- n. ‘sacrifice’ — Go. aibr n. ‘sacrificial animal’, OE tiber, tifer n. ‘sacri-

A word whose reconstruction poses many problems: 1. the attested Go.
form aibr does not match the anlaut of OHG zebar and OE tifer; and 2. the
vowel length of OE fer is ambiguous. To my mind, these difficulties are
best resolved by starting from OHG zebar, emending Go. aibr to tibr (cf.
Lehmann 1986: 13), and assuming that OE tifer has a short vowel. (Note
that the appurtenance of the sometimes connected hapax ON tivurr (=
tifurr?), meaning either ‘sacrifice’ or ‘god’, remains uncertain.) The resulting
*tibra- < PIE *dip-ré- may together with Gr. 5etrvov have split off from a PIE
heteroclitic *déip-r, gen. *dip-n-ds.

*bagén- wv. ‘to be silent’ — Go. bahan wv. ‘id.’, ON begja wv. ‘id.’, Far. tiga

An old stative formation identical to Lat. tacére. In Go. bahan the effects of

*baggon- w.v. ‘to silence’ — ON pagga w.v. ‘id.’, Nw. tagga w.v. ‘id.’ >

An interesting formation. Formally, the verb looks like the iterative (3sg.
*bakkopi, 3pl. *bagunanpi < *tHk-néhz-ti, *tHk-nh2-énti) to *pagén-, but se-

subcaudal bodypart (pace Katz 1998).

*begna- m. ‘retainer’ — ON pegn m. ‘thane, franklin, freeman, man; liege-

A derivation from the verb *pegjan- ‘to request, beg’. The original mean-
ing was ‘retainer’, i.e. an aristocratic dependant of a king or nobleman who
gives service in return for patronage. The word is traditionally compared to
Gr. tékvov n. ‘child’, a formation belonging to tiktw ‘to give birth’ < *ti-tk-e-
(cf. Torp 1909: 177; Pokorny IEW: 1057; Shields 2006). The implied pro-
to-form *tek-no-, however, would depending on the place of the accent have
yielded either **pehna- or **bekka- (the latter with Kluge’s law). This not
being the case, the etymology must be rejected.

*béka- m. ‘drifting seaweed’ — WFri. obs. teek ‘id.’, NFri. (F) tiak, (Hlg., Mo.,

An etymologically obscure word (cf. Sjélin 2006: 231) found only dialec-

source of the forms with *f Alternatively, it is possible that the adoption of
the word by the non-Frisian population took place before the change of *b
to d in the Frankish and Saxon dialects, thus resulting in daak or deek. The

*bewén- w.v. ‘to subdue’ — Go. ga-biwan w.v. ‘to subdue, subjugate’, ON pjd

The common opinion on the derivation of the verb is that it was derived
from *bewa- ‘servant’ (q.v.), and the verb indeed means ‘to enslave’ in both
Gothic and Old English. However, the Old Norse verb pjd has an additional,

further supported by OE ge-béon ‘to tame, oppress’ < *bewdjan- and the
marginally attested adjective OE béow adj. ‘subservient’, OS thio-liko adv.

which *pewa- ‘slave’ may be a nominalization. It thus seems conceivable

primary sense ‘bound, unfree, tamed’. This is a serious complication re-
garding the standard etymology of the word, which consists of a connection
with the PIE root *tekv- ‘to run’, cf. Skt. tdkti ‘to rush, fly’, Av. tacaiti ‘id’,

568 *wajju-

uuaisdus (> Fr. guéde) and the ablauting formations OE weard m. ‘vermil-

(Zohary and Hopf 2000: 209). Geographically, the word is limited to the

No certain extra-Gm. etymology: the OED mentions the connection with

*wébna- ~ *wépna- n. ‘weapon’ — Go. wepn* n. ‘id.’, ON vdpn, vakn, vamnn.
‘id’, Icel. vopn, obs. vokn n. ‘id.’, Far. vdpn, vakn n. ‘weapon; whaling lance’,

A Germanic word displaying two different stems, viz. *wébna- (cf. ON
vdmn, OE wémn) and *wépna- (cf. ON vdpn, OE wépn, OFri. wépen, OS
wapan, OHG wafan): the Nordic forms with k, cf. Icel. vokn, Far. vakn (with

The thematicization happened at a surprisingly early stage, however, as

l.c.), probably through a meaning ‘to brandish’. This is especially attractive
in view of Du. obs. wappen w.v. ‘to strike, knock, cuff, G Rhnl. wappen w.v.
‘to cuff. For other explanations, see Blazek 2008.

*wlaiton- 591

we, obl. as pron. ‘id.’, Du. wij, we, obl. ons pron. ‘id.’, OHG wir, obl. uns, acc.

tain etymology. The connection with W gwrysg f. ‘branch’ < PCelt. *wre/isk-
is flawed, as this word is more likely to be related to gwreid ‘roots’ (see
under *wurti-). The derivation from *ured*-ske- (cf. Magnusson 1989: 790),
where *ured*- is taken to be a Schwebeablaut form of *uerd- ‘to grow’, is
even more unlikely.

*wrépu- m. ‘herd (of swine)’ — Go. wribus (for expected *wrepus) m. ‘id.’,
ODa. vrath ‘swineherd’, Da. vrdd c. ‘id.’, OE wr@d m. ‘herd; host’ > *uréhr-tu-
(1E) — Skt. vrata- m. ‘troop, herd’ < *urehr-to-.

596 *wrihan-

Also cf. ON rddi m. ‘boar’ < *wréban-, ON rdda ‘to have sex with’ <
*wrépdjan-(?) and Nw. reda, vreda w.v. ‘to be in heat’ < *wrépjan-.

*wrihan- m. ‘instep’ — MDu. wrijghe, wrijch, wrijf m. ‘id.’, Du. wreef c. ‘id’,
OHG riho m. ‘id.’, G Reihen m. ‘id.’ > *uréik-on- (1E) — Lith. rfeSas m., riega f.
‘instep, wrist, knuckle’ < *ureik-o- (with métatonie rude).

An ablauting n-stem nom. *wrihd, gen. *wrikkaz, dat. *wriheni < *uréik-on,
*urik-n-6s, *urik-én-i (Kroonen 2011a: 261-2). The zero grade forms are
attested in late and dialectal Germanic only, cf. Du. dial. wree, Swi. (Rhtl)
reaha < *wrihan- and Du. obs. wreeg < *wrigan-. Related to *wraiha- (q.v.).

*wrinan- s.v. ‘to howl’ — Nw. vrina s.v. ‘to howl; to bare one’s teeth’, Elfd.
rwaina s.v. ‘to howl, wail’ > *uréiH-ne- (IE?).

A strong verb, in association with *hrinan-, cf. ON hrina, Far. rina s.v. ‘to
cry, wail’. Related to OE wréne adj. ‘lascivious’ < *wrainja- and ODu. wrénisk
adj. ‘id.’ < *wrainiska-. Also cf. OHG reinnio, OS wrénio, MDu. wrene m. ‘stal-
lion’ < *wrainjan-.

*wringan- s.v. ‘to wring, squeeze’ — OE wringan s.v. ‘to wring, twist’, E to
wring, OS ut-wringan s.v. ‘to squeeze out’, Du. wringen s.v. ‘to wring’, OHG
ringan s.v. ‘to wring; to wrestle’, G ringen sv. ‘id.’ > *uréng*-e- (NEUR) —
Lith. rangyti ‘to wind, bend’ < *urong'-eie-; Lith. rafigas m. ‘wrap, clew, ring’
< *urong'-o-.

On the basis of the WGm. forms, the verb is traditionally reconstructed as
*wringan-, which could be related to Lith. rangyti. There is a possibility,
however, that *wringan- replaced older *wrinhan-, a formation that perhaps
can be retrieved from Icel. rjd w.v. ‘to wrestle, fight; to move, tear’ (related
to Far. riggin adj. ‘fickle; resentful’?). This would imply a PIE root *urenk-
rather than *ureng*-. However, Icel. rjd can alternatively be reconstructed
as *rewan- (q.v.). See also *wranga-, *wrankjan- and *wrung6n-.

*wrinpla-(?) m. ‘a certain plant’ — Gutn. rind ‘clubmoss’, ME writhel ‘wild
lettuce(?)’ (GM).

Etymology uncertain. It is possible that both the formations Gutn. rind (<
*wrinda-) and ME writhel (< *wrinpla-) were derived from a root *wrinp- ‘to
wind’. This could technically be a nasal infixed root belonging to the strong
verb *wriban- ~ *writan- ‘to twist’ (q.v.).

*writan- s.v. ‘to carve’ — OE writan s.v. ‘to write; to carve’, OFri. writa s.v.
‘to write’, WFri. write s.v. ‘to tear; to ache, hurt’, OS writan s.v. ‘to tear; to
write’ > *uréid-e- (GM).

A strong verb derived from a further unknown root *ureid-. It merged
with *ritan- ‘to tear’ (cf. Du. rijten s.v. ‘id.’) in Old Norse and Old High Ger-

*writi- 597

man, Where initial *w was lost in front of r. Also cf. *writi-, *wraitjan- and
*writton-.

*writi- m. ‘stroke’ — Go. writs m. ‘id.’, MDu. ret m. ‘crack, fissure, lacuna’,
OHG riz m. ‘scratching, line, letter’, G Ris m. ‘crack, scratch’ (DRV).
An i-stem to the strong verb *writan- (q.v.).

*writton- w.v. ‘to carve, write’ — OHG rizz6n, rezzon w.v. ‘id.’, G ritzen w.v.
‘id.’ > *urid-néh2- (GM).

The iterative to *writan- (q.v.). It is possible that the *t of the strong verb
continues *-tt-, thus pointing to influence from this iterative.

*wripan- ~ *writan- s.v. ‘to twist’ — ON rida s.v. ‘to turn, ring, tie’, OSw.
vripa s.v. ‘to ring’, Elfd. rwaida sw. ‘to turn, twist, ring’, OE wriden s.v. ‘to
twist, ring’, E writhe s.v. ‘id’, MDu. writen s.v. ‘to twist, ring, wrap’, OHG
ridan s.v. ‘to wind, turn’, MHG riden s.v. ‘to wind, wrap’ > *uréit-e- (NEUR) —
Lith. riésti (rieciw) ‘to bend, curve, warp’, Latv. riest ‘to fall off, shed, shoot,
sprout’ < *ureit-ie-; Lith. rietéti ‘to hatch’ < *ureit-eh;-; Lith. risti ‘to roll’,
Latv. rist ‘id.’ < *urit-.

The original meaning was ‘to twist’, which remarkably enough in both
Baltic and Germanic developed into ‘to squirm’ (cf. WPhal. vrissen ‘worm’ <
*wrip-man- and Lith. rietéti ‘to hatch’) as well as ‘to sprout’ (cf. OE wridian
‘to bud’, Latv. riest ‘to sprout’). MDu. writen continues *writan- from
Pre-Gm. *writtan-, a variant whose geminate implies that it was influenced
by an iterative *writtdn-, cf. Nw. ritla w.v.‘to swerve’. See also *wraipa-.

*wrot- f. ‘root’ — ON rét, p. reetr f. ‘id’, Far. rét, pl. rgtur f. ‘id’, OSw. rot f.
‘id.’, Elfd. ruot, pl. ryéter f. ‘id.’ (EUR?).

A root noun usually reconstructed as PGm. *wrét-. The loss of the initial
*w is unexpected in East Norse, however. This means that the standard
etymological connection with *wurti- ‘root’ can only be maintained by as-
suming ad hoc deletion of *w.

*wrungon- f. ‘snare’ — Go. wruggo f. ‘snare, noose’ (DRV).
Also cf. MDu. wronc m. ‘noose, wreath; twisting; anger’, Du. wrong c.
‘braid’ < *wrunga-. Derived from *wringan- (q.v.).

*wulan- s.v. ‘to well up, boil, seethe’ — Go. wulan sv. ‘to boil, be hot’ >
*ulH-e- (IE).

A zero-grade present closely related to *wallan- (q.v.). With the same
vocalism, cf. ON olmr adj. ‘raging’ < *wulma- and Nw. olle f. ‘wave’ <
*wulldén-, which is fully parallel to OCS viena ‘id.’ < *ulH-nehz-.

598 *wulfa-

*wulfa- m. ‘wolf — Go. wulfs m. ‘id.’, ON ulfr m. ‘id’, Far. uilvur m. ‘id.’, Elfd.
ulv m. ‘id.’, OE wulfm. ‘id.’, E wolf, OS wulf, wolf m. ‘id.’, Du. wolf c. ‘id.’, OHG

NP gurg ‘id.’; Gr. AbKog m. ‘id’, Lat. lupus m. ‘id’, Lith. vilkas, Latv. vilks m.
‘id.’, OPru. wilkis ‘id.’ OCS vileke, Ru. volk, SCr. vak m. ‘id.’, Alb. ujk m. ‘id.’.

The IE word for ‘wolf. In Germanic, the expected form would be
**wulhwaz, but the *k was changed into *p as in *fimfe ‘5’ < *penke and
*werpan- ‘to throw’ < *uérg¥-e-. This change seems to have taken place after
resonants in words with initial labials. See also *wulgi- ~ *wulbjo-.

*wulgi- ~ *wulbjo- f. ‘she-wolf — ON ylgr, ylgja f. ‘id.’, Elfd. ylva f. ‘id.’, OHG
wulpa f. ‘id.’, MHG wiilpe f. ‘id.’ => *ulk-ih2- (1E) — Skt. vyki- f. ‘she-wolf, Lith,
vilké f. ‘id.’, Ru. voléica; SCr. vucica f. ‘id.’ < *ulkw-ih2-.

The feminine counterpart of *wulfa- ‘wolf (q.v.). ON ylgr continues the
most archaic form, viz. *wulgiz. (According to Kortlandt 1997a, it proves
that the unrounding of *kw was prior to Verner’s law, but see the introduc-
tion §2.2.4.) The form *wulbjo(n)-, as supported by OHG wulpa and Elfd.
ylva, is more secondary, but still must have adopted the p (< *k”) from the
masculine form before the operation of Verner’s law.

*wulhja- m. ‘haze’ — ON ylr m. ‘warmth’, Nw. g/ m. ‘(mild) warmth; steam’
= *ulk-i- (1E) — To Arm. gatjadj. ‘lukewarm’ < *ul(H)-i-?

To be derived either from *wulja- (Magnusson 1989: 1165; Olsen 1999:
204) or from *wulhja-. The latter option is supported by the potential link
with Icel. volgur adj. ‘lukewarm’ < *walga-. Also cf. Icel. yija w.v. ‘to heat up’,
Nw. glja w.v. ‘to radiate heat’ < *wul(h)jdjan-.

*wulk/gon- w.v. ‘to be nauseated’ — Icel. dlga ‘to foam, swell, seethe’ (also
cf. dlgra w.v. ‘to ferment, boil’), Far. ulka w.v. ‘to vomit, be sick’, Nw. ulka
w.v. ‘to be nauseated, feel sick’, G wulgern w.v. ‘to be nauseated’ >
*ulgh-néh2- (IE?).

The iterative to *walkan- (q.v.), originally conjugated as 3sg. *wulkopi,
3pl. *wulgunanpi < *ulg'-néhz-ti, *ulg-nh2-énti. The geminate of the singular
was apparently adopted by the strong verb.

*wullo- f. ‘wool’ — Go. wulla f. ‘id.’, ON ull f. ‘id.’, Far. ull f., OE wull f. ‘id.’, E

*wulpu- 599

Unlike e.g. Skt. urna- and Lat. lana, the Germanic word with its double /
points to a suffix-stressed form *Hulh1-néhz-. This accentual mobility is an
additional argument for reconstructing a consonant stem, which is already
implied by the potential suffix ablaut of Hitt. hulana- < *Hulhy-en-. The al-
ternative is to reconstruct a mobile neuter o-stem *Huflh;-n-om, pl.
*Hulhy-n-ého.

*wulpu- m. ‘glory’ — Go. wulpbus m. ‘id.’ > *ul-tu- (EUR) — Lat. vultus m. ‘fa-

*wuldra- < *ul-tré- / *ul-dtro-.

*wuna(n)- adj. ‘accustomed’ — OE ge-wun adj. ‘id.’, OS gi-wono, gi-wuno adj.

‘id.’ > *Hunhr-on- (1E) — OCS unii comp. ‘better’ < *Hunh1-iHo-.

A zero-grade formation closely related to *wana- 2 (q.v.).

*wunda- adj. ‘wounded’ — Go. wunds adj. ‘id.’, OE wund adj. ‘id.’, OS wund

*wunén- w.v. ‘to be used to’ — Go. un-wunands adj. ‘discontent, unhappy’,

Astative to the adjective *wuna(n)- (q.v.).

*wunni-f. ‘suffering’ — Go. wunnsf. ‘id.’ (DRV).
An i-stem derived from the strong verb *winnan- (q.v.).

*wunskjan- w.v. ‘to wish’ — ON eskja wv. ‘id.’, OE wyscan wy. ‘id’, E to

*wurda- n. ‘word’ — Go. waurd n. ‘id.’, ON ord n. ‘id.’, OE word n. ‘id’, E

*wurti- 601

*wurti- f. (medicinal) root; herb’ — Go. waurts f. ‘root’, ON urt f. ‘id.’, OE
wyrt f. ‘plant, herb’, OS wurt f. ‘id.’, MDu. wort f. ‘id.’, OHG wurz f. ‘root, herb,

A word whose PIE root can hardly be reconstructed. The presumably
related PGm. *wr6t- together with Lat. radix presupposes *urehzd-, but OlIr.

which points to PCelt. *wradi- (< *urehzd-i- with pretonic shortening or with
*CRHC- > *CRaC-). The appurtenance of Gr. paduE, -ikog m. ‘branch, twig;
palm leaf is uncertain. Within Germanic, also cf. the compound OE
wyrt-wala m. ‘id.’, MDu. wortel(e) m./f. ‘id.’, Du. wortel c. ‘id.’, OHG wurzala f.
‘id.’, G Wurzel f. ‘id.’ < *wurti-wala/on- “root-stick” (cf. *walu-).

*wur pi- f. ‘mound, elevation’ — ON urd f. ‘heap of stones fallen from a hill’,

= *hzur-ti- (DRV).

A ti-stem to the root of *warjan- (q.v.). Related to Elfd. ward m. ‘long or
high mountain’ < *warpa-?

The order of the languages is as follows: Germanic (Gothic; Old Norse;
Icelandic; Faroese; Norwegian; Elfdalian; Old & Modern Swedish (including
Gutnish); Old, Early & Modern Danish; Old, Middle & Modern English; Old
Frisian as well as Modern West, East & North Frisian; Old Saxon; Middle &
New Low German; Old Low Franconian & Old Dutch followed by Middle,
Early & Modern Dutch; Old, Middle & New High German plus Swiss German
and Lombardic); Other Indo-European languages: Anatolian (Hittite;
Luvian; Lycian); Tocharian (A & B); Italic (Oscan & Umbrian; Old, Classical,
Vulgar, Middle and Neo-Latin; Italian; Lombard; Spanish; Portuguese; Old,
Middle & Modern French); Venetic; Celtic (Celtiberian; Gaulish; Old, Middle
& Modern Irish (including Scottish Gaelic); Old, Middle & Modern Welsh;
Old, Middle & Modern Breton; Old, Middle & Modern Cornish);
Balkan-Indo-European (Mycenaean; Ancient & Modern Greek; Phrygian
Albanian; Armenian); Thracian; Iranian (Old & Young Avestan, Old, Middle
& New Persian; Sogdian; Khotanese; Pashto; Wakhi; Kurdish; Ossetic);
Indic (Sanskrit); Slavic (all variants of Church Slavonic plus Old Church
Slavonic; Serbian & Croatian; Slovene; Old and Modern Russian; Ukrainian;
Byelorussian; Old & Modern Czech; Slovak; Old & Modern Polish); Baltic
(Old Prussian; Old & Modern Lithuanian; Latvian); Non-Indo-European
languages (in alphabetical order).

With minor variations, the alphabetical order of the cited forms is
everywhere (except for Greek) the one of the Roman alphabet, and
whenever possible, I have brought it in agreement with the official (Roman)
orthographies of the modern standard languages.
